data.reasoning: Both models reviewed all 3 files in the AUR repository (PKGBUILD, .SRCINFO, LICENSE). The PKGBUILD is a standard Python package build that fetches a versioned tarball from the official GitHub repository with a pinned SHA-256 checksum, uses standard build tools (python -m build, python -m installer), and contains no suspicious patterns. The .SRCINFO is standard metadata. The LICENSE is a standard ISC license text. The only disagreement was caused by a transient API error (HTTP 400) in the qwen model when auditing the LICENSE file, which is trivially safe as it contains no executable code.
data.disagreement_analysis: The disagreement was caused by a tool error (HTTP 400 BadRequestError) in the qwen model when attempting to audit the LICENSE file. This resulted in an 'inconclusive' verdict for that file, which cascaded to an overall 'inconclusive' package verdict. The deepseek model successfully audited the same LICENSE file and correctly identified it as a standard ISC license with no security concerns. The disagreement is not based on any actual security analysis difference.
learnings: Tool errors (API failures) on trivially non-executable files (LICENSE, README, etc.) should not cascade to an overall 'inconclusive' package verdict. The system should recognize that license files and documentation cannot contain executable payloads.
When one model fails due to a transient error and another model succeeds on the same files, the successful model's verdict should be trusted for those files, especially for non-executable content.
Consider implementing a fast-path for obviously safe file types (LICENSE, README, .txt) that bypasses LLM analysis entirely, reducing both cost and failure points.
